title: The cost of mercy
hookLine: Dorothy Day lived the works of mercy at a personal cost

cards: Soup on a stove in a New York kitchen. Coffee for whoever comes in off the street.

Beds upstairs, not enough of them, and a woman who lives in the same house as the people she feeds, eats the same soup, and shares the same bathroom. Her name was Dorothy Day, and you met her on day nine hundred thirteen.
With a friend, Peter Maurin, she started a newspaper called the Catholic Worker, and then houses of hospitality where people in need could simply stay. Yesterday's charity was organized and wide.
Today, what it costs the one who gives.

teach.b: Her rulebook was Matthew's Gospel, where Jesus lists the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner, and says that whatever is done for them is done for him.

"I was a stranger, and you took me in," in the Douay-Rheims. The Church gathers those deeds into the corporal works of mercy, and Day treated them less as good ideas and more as a daily schedule. Then the cost.
Living with the poor meant noise, smells, theft, people who were sick or angry or drunk, and very little privacy. It meant being tired most of the time. She went to jail for her protests.
Mercy, in her house, wasn't something you dropped off on your way somewhere nicer. So why doesn't the cost cancel it?

teach.h: A SAINT IS TOO EASY TO DISMISS.
teach.b: The story is told that Day didn't want to be called a saint, because a saint is easy to admire and easy to dismiss. If she was special, nobody else had to do it.
She wanted the works of mercy to look ordinary and within reach. Her cause for canonization has been opened anyway, and she is now called a Servant of God. Now the carry.
Some mercy costs nothing, and it's still good.

teach.h: THE COST MAKES IT A GIFT.
teach.b: But Day's life suggests that when mercy starts to cost you, sleep, comfort, money, the good opinion of others, that's often when it stops being a gesture and starts being love.

teach.h: I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.
teach.b: Not suffering for its own sake. The cost is what makes it a gift.

how: Catholics practice the corporal works of mercy through soup kitchens, prison and hospital visits, and houses of hospitality like those of the Catholic Worker movement, which Dorothy Day co-founded.

games.q: what does “the cost of mercy” mean?
o: mercy that asks something real of the giver
the price a charity charges for its help
the money a parish sets aside for the poor

games.q: the cost of mercy — tap the pairs.
p: lived in the house with those she fed
started the Catholic Worker with her
her title now, as her cause goes on

s: Dorothy Day ran her houses from a separate, comfortable home
she lived in the same house as the people she fed.
the corporal works of mercy draw on a list in Matthew's Gospel
the hungry, the thirsty, the stranger, the naked, the sick and the prisoner.
the story goes that Day wanted to be called a saint
she didn't want it: a saint is easy to admire and easy to dismiss.

games.q: you've started a house that feeds people. it's loud, crowded and exhausting. where do you live?
o: in the house, with the people you feed.
you hire staff and visit on weekends.
games.why: Dorothy Day lived in the house of hospitality herself, sharing its noise and its soup.

practice: Let Matthew's list walk slowly past, hungry, thirsty, stranger, naked, sick, prisoner, and notice which one tugs at you.

Ask what a kindness there would really cost, an hour, a visit you've put off, a meal with someone hard to be around, and if there's reluctance, look at it honestly. If you pray, ask for the nerve to pay it.

wordCard.voice: The cost of mercy. Dorothy Day's lesson: the works of mercy lived at a price, and the price turns a gesture into a gift.

orig.note: Latin: mercy. the Latin Bible calls the merciful of Matthew 5:7 misericordes.

carryVoice: Your line: the cost is the point. Dorothy Day lived it under one roof with the people she fed. Until tomorrow.
